notes: This dataset compares 24 GB GPUs that remain relevant to local LLM inference because capacity, bandwidth, software maturity, power, and acquisition cost differ materially.

Manufacturer specifications are treated separately from retailer observations. Prices are point-in-time Canadian observations and are not normalized across new, refurbished, in-stock, and out-of-stock conditions.
Model-fit guidance is approximate and depends on quantization, context/KV cache, runtime overhead, batching, and whether weights are fully GPU-resident.

hardware.reference_form_factor: 313 mm length, 138 mm width, 3-slot Founders Edition
hardware.reference_power_connectors: 2x PCIe 8-pin via included 12-pin adapter on Founders Edition
hardware.software_lifecycle: Ampere remains an ongoing CUDA architecture in NVIDIA's current CUDA architecture matrix; unlike Pascal/Volta, it is not capped at CUDA 12.x.
hardware.model_size_practicality: Strong single-card target for 7B-14B models at high precision/longer context and many 20B-35B-class models at 4-5 bit quantization when runtime overhead and KV cache fit. Larger models require CPU offload or multiple GPUs.
quantization_compatibility: FP16/BF16/INT8 workload support is runtime dependent
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: High. Mature CUDA ecosystem, 24 GB capacity, 936 GB/s bandwidth and widespread community support continue to make used RTX 3090 cards useful inference nodes.
hardware.multi_gpu_notes: Two-card and larger systems are common, but framework tensor-parallel behavior and NVLink use are application-dependent; do not assume transparent pooled VRAM.
physical_constraints: Large 3-slot reference card; partner cards may be larger
Used cards may have unknown thermal/mining history
hardware.off_grid_notes: Excellent performance and bandwidth, but 350 W board power makes sustained solar/battery operation materially harder than 70-230 W alternatives. Power limiting can improve practicality but is workload-specific and should be benchmarked separately.
hardware.cost_efficiency_notes: The key opportunity is secondary-market pricing, not current inflated reseller stock. Recent Canadian refurbished listings span roughly CA$800-2,000 depending on stock and seller, so condition and availability must be retained with every observation.

pricing.note: MSI RTX 3090 Suprim X 24G refurbished listing. Marketplace pricing is unusually high and should not be treated as fair used-market value.
Recent out-of-stock refurbished RTX 3090 listings around CA$799.99 provide a useful acquisition target/floor reference, not a currently orderable price.

hardware.reference_form_factor: 2.5-slot reference class; partner designs vary and can exceed 3 slots
hardware.reference_power_connectors: 2x 8-pin on AMD reference specification; partner cards may differ
hardware.software_lifecycle: AMD's current ROCm 7.2 Windows support matrix lists RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100) with supported Runtime and HIP SDK. Linux ROCm support is also established, but exact framework/library support remains release-dependent.
hardware.model_size_practicality: 24 GB capacity is suitable for many 20B-35B-class models at 4-5 bit quantization when context/KV cache fit. 70B-class dense models generally require partial CPU offload, aggressive quantization, or multiple GPUs.
quantization_compatibility: PyTorch quantized paths depend on ROCm/runtime support
Do not assume CUDA-only GPTQ/AWQ kernels have equivalent AMD support
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: High for users willing to validate ROCm/Vulkan runtime compatibility. The 960 GB/s memory bandwidth is particularly attractive for memory-bound token generation.
physical_constraints: Partner cards can be physically very large
ROCm support is materially better than early RDNA3 launch-era guidance but remains framework/version dependent
hardware.off_grid_notes: Bandwidth is excellent, but 355 W TBP is a large continuous load. Better suited to surplus-solar/high-production windows than always-on battery operation unless power-limited and benchmarked.

pricing.note: Current Canadian search result showed an orderable ASRock 24 GB OEM listing at CA$1,399.99. Partner-card pricing varies substantially.
Out-of-stock refurbished observation retained as a secondary-market target, not current availability.

hardware.form_factor: 4.4 in high x 10.5 in long, dual-slot, full-height
hardware.software_lifecycle: Ampere remains supported by current CUDA architecture/toolkit generations.
hardware.model_size_practicality: Similar 24 GB model-capacity envelope to RTX 3090/RX 7900 XTX, but lower 230 W board power, ECC memory, active dual-slot workstation cooling and professional form factor improve deployment practicality.
hardware.llm_inference_suitability: High when acquired at sensible secondary-market pricing. It sacrifices raw bandwidth versus RTX 3090/RX 7900 XTX but delivers substantially better bandwidth-per-watt and denser dual-slot packaging.
hardware.multi_gpu_notes: NVIDIA documents two RTX A5000 cards connected by NVLink with 48 GB combined memory for applications that explicitly support NVLink; this is not transparent universal VRAM pooling.
physical_constraints: Dual-slot full-height but easier to integrate than many 3-4 slot gaming cards
230 W TBP still requires meaningful system cooling
Current new retail channel pricing is extremely poor value
hardware.off_grid_notes: At 230 W, A5000 is materially easier to sustain from batteries/solar than 350-355 W 24 GB gaming GPUs while retaining 768 GB/s bandwidth. Used acquisition price is the deciding factor.
hardware.cost_efficiency_notes: Current new Canadian reseller listings around CA$5,299 are not competitive for local LLM use. The card belongs in the catalog primarily as a secondary-market target where its ECC, 230 W TBP and NVLink can become attractive.

pricing.note: Current new marketplace listings are around CA$5,299 and are explicitly classified as poor value for local LLM acquisition.
